title: The Savoy Ballroom crowds and the grind at the Terrace
summary: A Chicago Savoy engagement drew a line around the block on 47th Street, and the Terrace job was seven nights with three shows, two broadcasts and little pay.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: We didn't really prosper but what happened, the Terrace prospered. We had to stand in line, Stanley. We did a thing at the Savoy Ballroom.

Yeah, that's 47th Street. It's Martin Luther King Boulevard now. It was 47th Street and South Parkway so we came in after a tour. It was absolutely disastrous. So we had an engagement to do at the Terrace. One thing we had was to ... and the fellow that talked about you, was a great critic I always from the American thought, I can't remember his name.

He was with the Chicago American and I always thought it always helped, we had radio time and all those things happened. So we got into going to the Savoy Ballroom that night and we had a bus going up there. And there were people who were past lined from the Savoy pass the Regal, there's a Walgreen Drugstore around the corner and around the block on 47th street. Where do you think they're going? They were going to hear us. And, those people to get in, they tore the doors down. And I think you might have something to do with it. ... And, jazz was appreciated. Now, Goodman, Benny was working -- I think he followed the probably was the Duke in Congress. So, it was one of those things. The music was alive. Henderson's band was on the upswing. You know we had some things to do. And it was a

tremendous band. It was a rough job. That was 7 nights a week and we did three shows a night, two broadcasts a night and ( ? ) they threw water on us from 6:45 until 7 o'clock on a Sunday afternoon. So, what the hell, it was a time when you, it was a challenge. It was well worth it. The money wasn't that good. It wasn't that good at all.
Well, the Grande Terrace didn't pay that well.
I mean I always heard that from Earl Hines.
